1:
The connecting particle resumes the charge of the previous chapter: Ellicott paraphrases it "in pursuance of my great charge, I proceed by special details," the first detail being that the congregation pray. Barnes takes "first of all" as primacy of importance rather than order of time, and reads it as addressed to everyone who leads in public prayer — which he thinks tells against a prescribed liturgy, since a bishop who had written the petitions would have no occasion to urge them. The four terms have resisted division. Clarke, following Macknight, assigns them to averting evils, obtaining needed good, pleading for others, and thanksgiving; Ellicott makes supplication a request for a particular benefit and so a species of the general word, intercession a drawing near into free and familiar speech, and thanksgiving the one form Trench says will survive in heaven, when all the rest have ceased in the fruition of what was asked. Calvin owns plainly that he does not thoroughly understand the difference between three of them, dismisses Augustine's ceremonial construction as "quite childish," and concludes that the heaping of words is meant to rouse a duty at which we are sluggish. Henry notes that Paul gives heads, not a form.

The scope is the point of the passage. Henry sees in it how far this religion was from being a sect, teaching a charity that prays not only for those of its own way but for all. Barnes sets it against the Jewish reckoning of the whole Gentile world as outside the covenant mercies, and asks whether a direction to give thanks on behalf of all does not imply that a way of salvation exists for all. Gill reads it as enjoined against a Jewish practice of cursing the Heathens and praying for none but themselves. Calvin states the objection in the mouth of the reluctant — why should we be anxious about the salvation of unbelievers? — and answers that the command simply refuses the limit. Chrysostom makes the priest the common father of all the world, and draws two advantages: hatred toward those without is done away, since no one can hate the man he prays for, and those prayed for are themselves made gentler by it. He asks what it was for persecutors to hear that those they scourged prayed fervently for them, and likens the Christian under ill-treatment to a father struck in the face by the child he is carrying, who loses nothing of his affection.

Kings are named as the hard case. Robertson observes that the class included Nero, who had already burned Rome and laid it on the Christians; Henry grants that these rulers were heathens and persecutors and holds that we must pray for them though we ourselves suffer under them. Chrysostom meets the suggestion that "all men" means all the faithful by pointing to the kings, and notes that Paul put the wider phrase first so it could not be read as flattery. Clarke gathers the practice from Cyprian before the proconsul and from Tertullian's plea for long life and a secure government; Ellicott adds Polycarp's charge to pray for persecutors and cruel enemies, and Josephus on the refusal to pray for Roman magistrates that helped bring on the war. Wesley points out that even the lowest magistrate does much good or harm. Ellicott finds a second object in the praying itself: habitual intercession would wear away thoughts of revolt, and no Christian was implicated in the rebellion that followed. Barnes denies that the tranquil life means comfort under protection: the Christian asks only not to be harassed for his religion. Chrysostom counts three wars, foreign, civil, and the war of the body against the soul, and asks what advantage the world's profound peace is to a man at war with himself. Both Ellicott and Robertson render the closing word gravity or decorum rather than honesty.
3:
The commendation looks backward before the ground of it is given. Clarke takes it of the praying itself: intercession for lawfully constituted authority is good in its own nature, useful to those who offer it and to the public, and its highest sanction is that it pleases God. Gill widens it to the whole manner of life just described and then to the prayer, good in itself and good in the sight of one who does not see as man sees, and accepted through Christ, by whom every sacrifice of prayer or praise is accepted. Both take "God our Saviour" of the Father; Gill distinguishes his saving of all men in providence from his saving of the elect in special grace. Ellicott notices where the title stands, immediately before the statement of boundless mercy that follows, and finds it singularly applicable there. Robertson notes only that the adjective rendered "acceptable" is a late word, known from inscriptions and papyri and used in the New Testament here and at 1 Timothy 5:4. Wesley draws a practical inference: if we ask why more are not converted, the answer is that we do not pray enough.

The clause that follows divides the commentators as sharply as anything in the letter. Barnes argues at length that the verb cannot carry the absolute sense it bears in the decree of creation, since what God wills in that sense is certainly done; it denotes rather desire, or what accords with his nature, as he wills that sickness be relieved and the oppressed go free, or as a parent wills the welfare of a child and makes provision for it, so that if the child is neither virtuous nor happy the fault is the child's. He rejects as well the reading that "all men" means some of every rank and class, on three grounds: that it strains the obvious sense, that the prayer commanded in the first verse is made for mankind without exception and this is given as the reason for it, and that the reasons added in the two following verses — one God, one Mediator, one ransom — are unlimited in the same way. Robertson glosses the verb narrowly as God's wish and will so far as he can influence men. Ellicott, willing to grant the width, still cautions against pressing the verse as a proof of universal redemption.

His point is that the will named is not a will to save all — had that been the sovereign will, all would have been saved — but a will that all should be saved; through the death of Christ all are rendered capable of salvation, redemption universal yet conditional, since God has limited it to an appointed condition that not all will meet. Gill takes the opposite road. The salvation willed, he insists, is no bare possibility, no offer, no placing of men in a salvable state, but a real and actual salvation determined beforehand and secured by God's appointment, by the covenant, and by the mission that effected it; a will resting on man's performance would mean that none might be saved, and that any who were would be saved of him that willeth. Clarke answers as bluntly from the other side, asking how any Christian soul, in the face of such a declaration, can suppose that God ever unconditionally and eternally reprobated any man. Wesley reads it of all seriously, not a part only and much less the smallest part, and adds that those who come to the knowledge are not compelled. On that phrase Robertson notes a compound meaning full knowledge, and suspects a guard against teachers who would lead the people astray; Clarke makes it acknowledgment, the receiving of the truth as the rule of faith and the model of life.
5:
Barnes builds the whole argument on singularity. God is the common Father of a race made of one blood, and the Mediator stands between God and men, not between God and a part of them; there is not one for kings and another for their subjects, one for the rich and another for the poor, one for the master and another for the slave, so that a servant may know himself regarded with the same interest as his owner. He and Wesley both turn the same word against the invocation of saints and of the Virgin, Wesley adding that the heathen likewise set up many mediators to pacify their superior gods. Robertson calls the one-God premise a regular Pauline argument for a universal gospel and glosses the noun as a late word for a middle man; Clarke, taking it as one whose office is to reconcile parties at enmity, cites Suidas for the equivalent peace-maker, and observes that such reconciling required a sacrifice from the peace-maker. Gill reads the unity as one toward men rather than a statement about the divine essence — one Creator, one providential preserver, one covenant God of Jew and Gentile alike — and infers the duty of praying for all sorts.

On the human nature named in the same breath, Ellicott hears a silent refutation of teachers who would make the figure on the cross a phantom, and adds that the Messiah must have taken that nature before he could suffer the death which was the ransom. The word for ransom draws the closest attention. Robertson takes it for a reminiscence of the Lord's own saying, notes that in the papyri the preposition used is the ordinary one for substitution where benefit is involved while the prefix carries exchange, so that the compound holds both, and thinks Paul may have coined it. Clarke defines it as the redemption of life by life and quotes Schleusner's rendering, that by his death he freed all from the power and punishment of vice; Wesley says a like or equal is given, an eye for an eye, and that the dignity of the person redeeming made it more than equivalent. Clarke then lays out five steps — one God, creator of all, his kindness revealed to all, his will that all be saved, a mediator provided for all — and concludes that as surely as God created all men, so surely Christ died for all.

Gill grants the ransom was given for all and denies that "all" means every individual, since then all would be freed and saved; otherwise, he argues, either the price is paid in vain or God receives a sufficient satisfaction and still refuses to release the captive. Ellicott, for his part, describes the Mediator yielding himself of his own free will, his life in exchange for forfeited lives, and calls the teaching irreconcilable with any theology that lets men approach the Father without pleading that death. The clause about the testimony has been read many ways. Clarke sets out the Vulgate's bare rendering beside those of Macknight, Wakefield and Rosenmüller, records a single Cambridge manuscript that reads mystery for testimony and is supported by no other copy or version; his own sense is that the ransom was to be testified to every nation in the times that seemed best to divine wisdom. Barnes agrees, adding that the truth had gone unrecognised while salvation was thought to reach the heathen only through becoming a Jew. Barnes and Clarke agree that the verb rendered ordained means placed or appointed and implies no laying on of hands; Robertson observes that here alone Paul calls himself a teacher of the Gentiles. Ellicott finds the vehemence of the disclaimer aimed not at his own rank but at the magnitude of the message, an offer made not to a people but to a world.
8:
The opening verb is milder than the one used of God's will four verses earlier, and Barnes marks the difference: the earlier word denotes active volition, this one a willingness or desire. Nobody takes it as diffidence. Ellicott calls it the expression of solemn apostolic authority rather than a wish, Wesley says it strongly expresses that authority, and Clarke, reasoning that Paul spoke nothing but what he had received, makes it equal to a command. Robertson reads the accusative as men in contrast to the women of the next verse, and the setting as public worship. Gill agrees that only men are mentioned because it is public prayer in the church that is in view, and is careful to add that prayer in house and closet is as much the duty and privilege of women. Ellicott supplies a local occasion: the larger liberty women had come to enjoy, and the honour won by such workers as Dorcas, Priscilla and Lydia, had bred a self-assertion in the Ephesian congregations that threatened disorder in worship, and Paul follows the synagogue rule. Robertson enters the plainest caveat of the group, that many now judge these conditions peculiar to Ephesus and Corinth.

"In every place" is read against a settled assumption about sacred ground. Barnes notes that the Jews supposed a special efficacy in prayer offered at the temple and the heathen thought the same of their own shrines, both supposing they came nearer God by approaching his abode. Clarke traces the narrowing and its collapse — first Jerusalem only, then the Holy Land, then the oratories built by rivers and the seaside once the nation was dispersed — and answers that all places belong to God's dominion; his own maxim is that a man should always have a praying heart, and such a heart will ever find a praying place. Gill sets the phrase against the rule that prayer made elsewhere must at least be directed toward the temple. Ellicott hears in it a memory of the words spoken to the woman of Samaria. Chrysostom faces the harder objection, that Christ told his disciples to shut the door and pray in secret, and answers that the command was against ostentation and not about location, since the same Lord who bade the left hand not know what the right was doing was regulating vainglory, not hands. Henry simply enumerates: closets, families, meals, journeys, and assemblies public or private.

The posture was common ground. Ellicott finds the lifted hands in Jewish practice and generally adopted by the early Christians, citing Clement of Rome; Robertson notes they stood to pray, and that the adjective for holy takes an unusual feminine form with hands. Clarke adds that the heathen spread their arms likewise, calls it an effort to embrace the assistance requested, and then presses the verb toward the laying of hands on a sin-offering, so that the man who prays comes to the altar and lays his hand on the Lamb. Chrysostom asks what holy means and answers: not washed with water, but free from covetousness, rapacity and violence, hands employed in almsgiving. Wesley makes the wrath excluded of any kind, against any creature, and counts every motion of the soul that is not according to love as wrath. The last word divides them. Barnes traces it from reckoning through reasoning to debate and takes it of clamorous contention, remarking how often theologians grow so heated for victory that they cannot pray together; Ellicott and Robertson likewise render it disputing. Clarke turns it inward instead, to the controversy of faith and unbelief in the breast of a timid believer, and Wesley makes it simply the contrary of faith. Chrysostom takes it as misgiving about being heard.
9:
The verb of willing has to be carried over from the previous verse, and Robertson records a grammarian's further claim that "when they pray" must be supplied with it — possible on the grammar, he allows, but hard to square with what follows. Barnes reads the whole passage as regulating the conduct of public worship rather than private life, then observes that the principle cannot be quarantined there: if a manner of dress is fitting in the sanctuary it is fitting anywhere, and what is wrong there would be difficult to defend elsewhere. Ellicott takes the same line from the other end, holding that the direction was never meant for ordinary dress in the world but explained to the Ephesian sisters that their place in the service was one of quiet attention, without a conspicuous dress or showy ornament that might catch the eye and draw the thoughts of fellow worshippers. Gill puts it that the women are to pray likewise, not leading or serving as the mouth of the church, but joining in with the same purity of heart and hand the men were charged with, and without murmuring or distrust.

Barnes builds his reading on the verb: the word is adorn, so ornament as such is not condemned. The world as God made it is full of beauty, and in every flower he has shown that he is not against decoration; the quarrel is only over what true ornament is for a creature in our situation. From this he draws a workable rule — the line is crossed when the outward decoration occupies the mind more than the virtues of the heart — and adds that there is no religion in a negligent appearance either, a woman being able to offend by inattention as truly as by excess. Robertson supplies the philology: the noun for apparel is a late one found nowhere else in the New Testament, a letting down, used of demeanour as well as of dress, and its adjective means well-arranged. Clarke reconstructs the garments themselves, the long stola girded beneath the breast and the mantle worn loose over it, notes that the Grecian dress was as modest as any ever invented, and then reports Kypke's contrary opinion that no garment is meant at all, the word coming rather from a verb to restrain and describing the government of the mind over dress and bearing alike.

Over the four things named the commentators part company. Wesley holds them expressly forbidden by name to every woman professing godliness, allows no exception, and says no art of man can reconcile the wilful violation of an express command with the Christian profession. Barnes will not have it that mere braiding is prohibited, or every use of gold and pearls, and argues that no exact rule can be given since much depends on age, rank and means. Ellicott fills in the practice, gold twined among the plaits of the hair and earrings, necklaces and bracelets worn in profusion by the ladies of a luxurious age, and points to a graver reason for modest demeanour given elsewhere, because of the angels. Clarke reaches for Homer's Euphorbus, whose ringlets, bound about with twine of gold and silver, swept the dust when he fell. On what should take their place there is no dispute. Henry makes good works the best ornament and of great price in God's sight, and would have the money laid out on piety and charity instead of fine clothes; Ellicott points to Dorcas of Joppa, full of good works and almsdeeds; Clarke recalls the Jewish matrons who cried to a bride that she needed no paint, no antimony, no braided hair, being most beautiful herself; Robertson sums it as good dress and good works combined. Gill reads the professed godliness as covering the whole of religion, inward and outward, on which these women had been baptized.
11:
Chrysostom hears the regulation extend from dress to speech, grounds the silence in the subjection the law imposed, and complains that the women of his own congregation talk more in church than in the market or at the bath. Ellicott adds that even questioning on difficult points was barred in the assembly, and notes that when the prohibition was renewed at Carthage the same council expressly allowed women to teach others of their own sex privately, the ability to instruct rustic women being required of a deaconess. Gill likewise restricts the ban to the church and leaves the house open, observing that Timothy owed much to the private teaching of his mother and grandmother. Clarke declines to argue the case here, points instead to Roman law, which removed women from every public office, and remarks that men in an assembly might interrupt a speaker with a question where women might not. Robertson traces the second verb to a vernacular word for playing the master, and then admits that modern Christians let women teach classes and that something seems not to be expressed here that would make it all clear. Wesley glosses the phrase in four words: of public teaching.

Two reasons are then given, and both are worked hard. On the first Barnes insists that bare priority of existence cannot be the argument, since that would give every older person authority over a younger; the force lies in the account itself, the woman formed from the man's side and given to him as a companion rather than a lord. Clarke locates the ground in the body instead, holding that man's robust frame fits him for public exertion and woman's plainly does not, and quotes a Greek line that nature does not grant a woman rule; Wesley states flatly that the woman was originally the inferior. On the second reason the readings diverge. Ellicott takes both as sinning but only Eve as deluded, the compounded verb conveying thoroughness. Robertson doubts the compound carries that weight against the simple verb used of Adam. Gill refuses every softening and holds that Adam was never deceived at all, having never conversed with the serpent and eaten knowingly out of fondness for his wife, that she might not die alone, his sin being the greater for it. Barnes reads a feebler resistance rather than a graver guilt, and grants that in many traits, and those the loveliest, woman is the superior.

The closing promise is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and Barnes catalogues the attempts. Some make it the whole of the maternal calling; one equates the noun with education, so that a woman reaches salvation by rearing her children well; another reads it as preservation from the impostors and luxury of the age. Barnes himself takes the consolation to be that salvation stands open to her on the same terms as to man, and rejects the messianic reading of Doddridge and Macknight as too refined, as not the plain sense of the word, and as untrue in fact, since bearing the Saviour no more saved Mary than his birth alone saves a man. Clarke holds exactly that rejected reading, following Macknight, that the sex is saved through the bringing forth of the Saviour; he objects that pious women die in childbed while worthless ones come through easily, and reads the change from singular to plural as showing the whole sex is meant. Ellicott finds the clue in the article, "through the childbearing," and reads the Incarnation. Robertson allows that this is true but thinks the emphasis falls on childbearing as woman's own function, in which she is saved rather than by it; Wesley has her carried safe through the danger and finally saved if she continues in loving faith. Clarke ends by denying that the act itself entitles anyone to anything: pain neither purifies nor atones.
